summary:
Echoes on the Moon & Mars is an interactive educational web application developed for the Abandoned but not Forgotten challenge. Many school-age learners and casual space fans only hear about active missions, while the retired landers, rovers, and flyers left behind on the Moon and Mars are rarely remembered. This project solves that gap by turning six iconic pieces of retired NASA hardware into clear, engaging stories: the Apollo 11 Eagle descent stage, Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle, Mars Pathfinder and Sojourner, Mars Rover Opportunity, InSight Mars Lander, and Ingenuity Mars Helicopter.

Visitors can filter missions by destination or search by crew, crater, or keyword. Opening any mission reveals its crew or engineering team, exact dates, resting coordinates, planned versus actual mission duration, why and how it was built, and what went wrong during operations. A three-step Mission Journey breaks down how each craft landed, worked, and ended, paired with live public-domain photography fetched from the NASA Image and Video Library API and a 10-question Explorer Quiz. By showing the real engineering grit behind silent spacecraft, Echoes on the Moon & Mars makes 55 years of space exploration accessible and inspiring for the next generation.
details:
What It Does and How It Works:

Echoes on the Moon & Mars is an interactive, story-driven web application designed to teach school-age learners and casual space enthusiasts about NASA's retired equipment on the Moon and Mars. It features six iconic missions: Apollo 11 Eagle Descent Stage, Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle, Mars Pathfinder and Sojourner, Mars Rover Opportunity, InSight Mars Lander, and Ingenuity Mars Helicopter.

Visitors can filter missions by destination (Moon or Mars) or search by astronaut, mission, or crater. Selecting any mission opens a clear Mission Dossier showing the crew or engineering team, exact dates and weekdays, resting coordinates with a one-click Copy button, and planned versus actual mission duration. Each story is written in approachable third-person narration alongside dedicated sections for "Why They Did It & How", "What Went Wrong", and a three-step "Mission Journey" (How It Landed, What It Did, How It Ended). The app also fetches live public-domain photography from the NASA Image and Video Library API with a full-screen photo viewer, and includes a 10-question randomized Explorer Quiz with three astronaut ranks and recent score tracking.

Benefits and Intended Impact:

Most educational resources focus only on active missions. By highlighting the engineering challenges, unexpected setbacks, and scientific discoveries of retired spacecraft, this project helps students understand how past missions paved the way for modern exploration.

Tools and Technologies Used:

Built as a responsive single-page web application using HTML5, Tailwind CSS, Vanilla JavaScript, and an HTML5 Canvas animated starfield, hosted on Vercel with open-source code on GitHub.

Creativity and Factors Considered:

To keep the experience accessible for young learners, technical jargon and dense data tables were replaced with plain-English storytelling, color-coded world badges, interactive step-by-step mission breakdowns, and an engaging quiz.
